- D. Mann–Whitney

**Answer: A.** One sample against a known value with σ unknown → one-sample t (a z-test needs σ known).


### M5-W8 · Hospital stay (days) in two independent wards; heavily right-skewed, n = 12 per ward. {#m5-w8}

**Tests:** Student t-test (equal variances); Wilcoxon / Mann-Whitney (non-parametric); chi-square test; chi-square goodness of fit; skewness

- A. Student t
- **B. Mann–Whitney (wilcox.test)  ← correct**
- C. Paired t
- D. χ² GOF

**Answer: B.** Small, skewed, independent groups → non-parametric Mann–Whitney.


### M5-W9 · Pain scores of 15 patients before and after physiotherapy; the differences are clearly non-normal. {#m5-w9}

**Tests:** paired t-test; Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Wilcoxon / Mann-Whitney (non-parametric); McNemar test

- **A. Wilcoxon signed-rank  ← correct**
- B. Mann–Whitney
- C. Welch t
- D. McNemar

**Answer: A.** Paired data with non-normal differences → wilcox.test(after, before, paired = TRUE).


### M5-W10 · Does a 6-sided die produce each face equally often? 120 rolls. {#m5-w10}

**Tests:** chi-square test; chi-square goodness of fit; Fisher's exact test

- A. χ² independence
- B. One-sample t
- **C. χ² goodness of fit  ← correct**
- D. Fisher

**Answer: C.** One categorical variable (face) against equal probabilities → GOF, df = 5.


# Module 6 · ANOVA, post hoc, two-way ANOVA, regression, diagnostics, categorical predictors, mixed models


## M6 · Part B · Written and R questions (model answers)


### M6-B1 · One-way ANOVA when the assumptions fail [15 marks] {#m6-b1}

**Tests:** t-test; Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Shapiro-Wilk normality test; QQ plot; Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Welch ANOVA; post hoc / multiple comparisons (Holm, Bonferroni); Kruskal-Wallis; eta squared (effect size); chi-square test; SD / variance; mean / median / mode; skewness; boxplot; missing values (NA); group summaries  
**Functions:** `aggregate()`, `aov()`, `boxplot()`, `etaSquared()`, `factor()`, `is.na()`, `kruskal.test()`, `leveneTest()`, `mean()`, `median()`, `oneway.test()`, `pairwise.t.test()`, `residuals()`, `sd()`, `shapiro.test()`, `summary()`  
**Data:** airquality

**Question**

Load the built-in `airquality` dataset. Does mean ozone concentration differ between the five months (May–September)? Use only rows with non-missing `Ozone`.

(a) Convert `Month` to a factor. Draw a boxplot and report n, mean, SD and median per month. [2]
(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1]
(c) Perform a one-way ANOVA and report F, both df, p and η². [3]
(d) Test normality of the residuals and homogeneity of variance. [3]
(e) Revise the analysis as required, justifying your choice. [3]
(f) Run Holm-corrected pairwise t-tests and say which months differ. [3]

**Model answer (code + interpretation)**

```{r}
library(car); library(lsr)
aq <- airquality[!is.na(airquality$Ozone), ]
aq$Month <- factor(aq$Month, labels = c("May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep"))
boxplot(Ozone ~ Month, data = aq, ylab = "Ozone (ppb)")
aggregate(Ozone ~ Month, aq, function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), median = median(x)))
#  May n 26 mean 23.6 sd 22.2 median 18 | Jun 9, 29.4, 18.2, 23 | Jul 26, 59.1, 31.6, 60
#  Aug 26, 60.0, 39.7, 52              | Sep 29, 31.4, 24.1, 23
a <- aov(Ozone ~ Month, data = aq); summary(a)     # F(4, 111) = 8.54, p = 4.8e-06
etaSquared(a)                                      # 0.235
shapiro.test(residuals(a))                         # W = 0.932, p = 1.8e-05 → non-normal
leveneTest(Ozone ~ Month, data = aq)               # F(4, 111) = 3.96, p = 0.0049 → unequal variances
kruskal.test(Ozone ~ Month, data = aq)             # chi-sq(4) = 29.27, p = 6.9e-06
oneway.test(Ozone ~ Month, data = aq)              # Welch F(4, 42.67) = 8.03, p = 6.4e-05 (agrees)
pairwise.t.test(aq$Ozone, aq$Month, p.adjust.method = "holm")
#        May     Jun     Jul     Aug
#  Jun 1.000     -       -       -
#  Jul 0.0003  0.051     -       -
#  Aug 0.0002  0.0499  1.000     -
#  Sep 1.000   1.000   0.0049  0.0039
```

**(a)** Mean ozone is about twice as high in July and August (59–60 ppb) as in May, June and September (24–31). Every month is right-skewed (mean > median in May, Aug, Sep), and the spread grows with the level (SD 18–24 vs 32–40). June has only 9 non-missing days. **(b)** H0: μ_May = μ_Jun = μ_Jul = μ_Aug = μ_Sep; H1: not all equal. **(c)** F(4, 111) = 8.54, p < .001, η² = .24. **(d)** Both assumptions fail. Residuals are non-normal (W = .93, p < .001; the QQ plot curves up at the right). Variances are unequal (Levene F(4, 111) = 3.96, p = .005; SD ratio 2.2), and group sizes are unequal (9 to 29), which makes ANOVA more sensitive to this. **(e)** Use the course fallbacks. Normality fails, so run Kruskal–Wallis (ANOVA.Rmd, "removing the normality assumption"): χ²(4) = 29.3, p < .001, so ozone levels differ by month. Variances are unequal, so also run Welch's ANOVA with `oneway.test()` (ANOVA lecture: "if not homogeneous, run the oneway.test()"): F(4, 42.7) = 8.03, p < .001. Both agree with the original ANOVA. **(f)** Holm-corrected pairwise t-tests: July and August are higher than May (p = .0003, .0002) and higher than September (p = .005, .004). July and August don't differ (p = 1), and neither do May, June and September. June vs August is borderline (p = .0499) and June vs July is not significant (p = .051), probably because June has only 9 days. These t-tests assume normality and equal variances, which failed here, so say that the pattern is supported by the Kruskal–Wallis and Welch results.

> Marking: descriptives with an observation about skew/spread (a); hypotheses (b); F with both df and η² (c); both tests named, with values and a verdict (d); a fallback that matches each failure (Kruskal–Wallis for normality, Welch for variance), with justification (e); Holm-corrected comparisons with the pattern described and the caveat about the failed assumptions (f).


### M6-B2 · Two-way ANOVA with an interaction [15 marks] {#m6-b2}

**Tests:** Shapiro-Wilk normality test; Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; interaction; eta squared (effect size); transformation (log / sqrt); SD / variance; group summaries  
**Functions:** `aggregate()`, `aov()`, `etaSquared()`, `interaction.plot()`, `leveneTest()`, `log()`, `residuals()`, `shapiro.test()`, `summary()`, `TukeyHSD()`, `with()`  
**Data:** warpbreaks

**Question**

The built-in `warpbreaks` data record the number of warp breaks per loom for two wool types (A, B) at three tension levels (L, M, H), 9 looms per cell.

(a) Report the six cell means and draw an interaction plot. Describe the pattern. [2]
(b) State the three null hypotheses tested by a two-way ANOVA. [2]
(c) Fit `breaks ~ wool * tension` and report each effect. [3]
(d) Report partial η² for each effect. [1]
(e) Check normality of residuals and homogeneity of variance across cells. Revise the analysis if required, and say whether the conclusions change. [4]
(f) Use Tukey's HSD on the interaction to identify which cell(s) drive it. [3]

**Model answer (code + interpretation)**

```{r}
library(car); library(lsr)
aggregate(breaks ~ wool + tension, warpbreaks, mean)
#        L     M     H
#  A  44.56 24.00 24.56
#  B  28.22 28.78 18.78
with(warpbreaks, interaction.plot(x.factor = tension, trace.factor = wool, response = breaks))
wb <- aov(breaks ~ wool * tension, data = warpbreaks); summary(wb)
#  wool          F(1, 48) = 3.77  p = 0.058
#  tension       F(2, 48) = 8.50  p = 0.00069
#  wool:tension  F(2, 48) = 4.19  p = 0.021
etaSquared(wb)        # partial: wool 0.07, tension 0.26, wool:tension 0.15
shapiro.test(residuals(wb))                          # W = 0.987, p = 0.82
leveneTest(breaks ~ wool * tension, warpbreaks)      # F(5, 48) = 2.89, p = 0.023 → unequal
wbl <- aov(log(breaks) ~ wool * tension, warpbreaks); summary(wbl)
#  wool p = 0.14   tension F(2, 48) = 7.78 p = 0.0012   wool:tension F(2, 48) = 3.26 p = 0.047
leveneTest(log(breaks) ~ wool * tension, warpbreaks)  # p = 0.74 → fixed
shapiro.test(residuals(wbl))                          # p = 0.26
TukeyHSD(wb, "wool:tension")
#  every comparison with A:L is significant: B:L-A:L -16.3 (p = .030), A:M-A:L -20.6 (.003),
#  B:M-A:L -15.8 (.040), A:H-A:L -20.0 (.004), B:H-A:L -25.8 (.0001); no other pair p < .05
```

**(a)** Breaks fall as tension increases, but not in the same way for each wool: wool A drops sharply from L (44.6) to M (24.0) and then levels off, while wool B stays around 28 at L and M and falls only at H (18.8). The lines cross between L and M: an interaction. **(b)** No main effect of wool (μ_A = μ_B averaged over tension); no main effect of tension (μ_L = μ_M = μ_H averaged over wool); no interaction (the tension effect is the same for both wools). **(c)** Tension F(2, 48) = 8.50, p < .001. Wool F(1, 48) = 3.77, p = .058 (not significant). Interaction F(2, 48) = 4.19, p = .021. **(d)** Partial η²: wool .07, tension .26, interaction .15. **(e)** Residuals are normal (p = .82), but cell variances differ (Levene p = .023). The course's fix for a violated assumption in a linear model is to transform the outcome (regression lecture: "If there is severe violation, transform the data. Eg: Log"), and `aov()` is a linear model. On log(breaks), Levene p = .74 and Shapiro p = .26, so both assumptions are met. Tension (p = .001) and the interaction (p = .047) remain significant and wool remains non-significant, so the conclusions don't change; the interaction is weaker. **(f)** The interaction is driven by one cell: wool A at low tension (44.6 breaks) is higher than every other cell (all p ≤ .04), and no other pair differs. So the "tension effect" is mainly wool A's problem at low tension.

> Marking: cell means + described pattern (a); all three H0s (b); F(df1, df2) and p for each line (c); partial η² (d); Levene on the *cells*, the transform, the re-check, and the comparison of conclusions (e); naming A:L as the source (f).


### M6-B3 · Multiple regression with diagnostics (Quiz 6 format) [15 marks] {#m6-b3}

**Tests:** Shapiro-Wilk normality test; Tukey HSD post hoc; chi-square test; linear regression (lm); heteroscedasticity test (ncvTest); VIF / multicollinearity; Cook's distance / influential points; linearity check; linear mixed model (lmer); transformation (log / sqrt); power / sample size; SD / variance  
**Functions:** `cooks.distance()`, `lm()`, `log()`, `na.omit()`, `ncvTest()`, `powerTransform()`, `residualPlots()`, `residuals()`, `shapiro.test()`, `summary()`, `vif()`  
**Data:** airquality

**Question**

Using `airquality` (complete cases of Ozone, Solar.R, Wind, Temp), fit a multiple linear regression with **Ozone** as the dependent variable and **Solar.R, Wind and Temp** as predictors.

(a) **Fit the model.** Write the fitted equation, report the overall F-statistic and its p-value, and interpret R² and adjusted R². [3]
(b) **Interpret the predictors.** Report coefficients and p-values; which contribute significantly at α = .05 after accounting for the others? Interpret their direction. [3]
(c) **Check model assumptions:** linearity, normality of residuals, homoscedasticity, independence, multicollinearity, influential observations. State your finding for each. [6]
(d) **Revise and conclude.** Propose and fit a revised model that addresses the violations, and write a short conclusion. [3]

**Model answer (code + interpretation)**

```{r}
library(car)
aq <- na.omit(airquality[, c("Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp")])    # n = 111
a1 <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp, data = aq); summary(a1)
#  (Intercept) -64.34   Solar.R 0.0598 (p = 0.011)   Wind -3.334 (p = 1.5e-06)   Temp 1.652 (p = 2.4e-09)
#  R² = 0.606, adj R² = 0.595, F(3, 107) = 54.83, p < 2.2e-16
residualPlots(a1)               # Wind p = 5.1e-07, Temp p = 0.0002, Tukey p = 7.2e-09 → curvature
shapiro.test(residuals(a1))     # W = 0.917, p = 3.6e-06 → non-normal (right tail)
ncvTest(a1)                     # chi-sq(1) = 5.38, p = 0.020 → heteroscedastic
# independence: one row per day, no repeated measures of the same unit → argue from the design
vif(a1)                         # 1.10, 1.33, 1.43 → fine
cd <- cooks.distance(a1); max(cd); sum(cd > 4/111)   # max 0.26 (day 117: Ozone 168), 6 above 4/N, none > 1
# revision
summary(powerTransform(a1))     # Box-Cox power 0.22, rounded 0.33 → cube root of Ozone
aq$oz3 <- aq$Ozone^(1/3)        # Box-Cox with power 1/3
aq$logWind <- log(aq$Wind)      # log of a predictor, as in the lecture: lm(log(y) ~ log(x) + ...)
a2 <- lm(oz3 ~ Solar.R + logWind + Temp, data = aq); summary(a2)
#  oz3 = 1.00 + 0.0022 Solar.R - 0.808 logWind + 0.0468 Temp;  R² = 0.705, adj 0.697, F(3, 107) = 85.2
shapiro.test(residuals(a2)); ncvTest(a2)   # p = 0.37, 0.31 → normality and variance fixed
residualPlots(a2)               # logWind p = 0.27, Temp p = 0.020, Tukey p = 0.022 → mild curvature left
```

**(a)** Ozone = −64.34 + 0.060 Solar.R − 3.33 Wind + 1.65 Temp. F(3, 107) = 54.8, p < .001. R² = .61: the predictors explain 61% of day-to-day variation in ozone. Adjusted R² = .59 is close, so there is little over-fitting. **(b)** All three are significant. Temperature: +1.65 ppb per °F (p < .001). Wind: −3.33 ppb per mph (p < .001), since wind disperses ozone. Solar radiation: +0.06 ppb per Langley (p = .011), since sunlight drives ozone formation. Each is adjusted for the other two.

| Check | Finding |
|---|---|
| Linearity | **Violated.** Curvature for Wind (p < .001) and Temp (p < .001); residual-vs-fitted is U-shaped (Tukey p < .001). |
| Normality | **Violated.** W = .92, p < .001; long right tail (a few very high-ozone days). |
| Homoscedasticity | **Violated.** ncvTest p = .020; residual spread grows with fitted ozone (funnel). |
| Independence | **Assumed from the design.** Each row is a different day; there are no repeated measurements of the same unit (the case where the regression lecture says to move to a mixed model). Consecutive days may share weather, which is a limitation. |
| Multicollinearity | VIFs 1.1–1.4: none. |
| Influence | Day 117 (Ozone 168, the maximum) has Cook's D = 0.26: the largest, above 4/N = .036 but below 1. Six days exceed 4/N. Worth a refit check, but none is extreme. |

**(d)** The regression lecture's fix for severe violations is to transform the data ("Log or Box-Cox or powerTransform"). `powerTransform()` estimates a Box-Cox power of 0.22, so model the cube root of Ozone; following the lecture's `lm(log(y) ~ log(x) + ...)` example, use log(Wind) for the curved wind effect. The revised model explains more variance (R² = .71 vs .61), and its residuals are normal (Shapiro p = .37) with constant variance (ncvTest p = .31). The wind curvature is gone (p = .27); slight curvature in Temp remains (p = .02), which should be reported. *Conclusion:* "Ozone rises with temperature and solar radiation and falls with wind speed, with the wind effect strongest at low speeds. The original linear model was significant (R² = .61) but violated linearity, normality and constant variance. A model for the cube root of ozone with log wind speed fixes normality and constant variance and explains 71% of the variance; mild curvature in temperature remains. Limitations: complete cases only (111 of 153 days), consecutive days may not be independent, one summer of one city, and observational data."

> Marking mirrors Quiz 6: equation + F + R²/adjusted R² (a); coefficients with p and direction (b); one mark per assumption, each with a test or plot *and* a verdict (c); a sensible revision that is re-checked, plus a conclusion with limitations (d).


### M6-B4 · Regression with a categorical predictor [10 marks] {#m6-b4}

**Tests:** ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; post hoc / multiple comparisons (Holm, Bonferroni); eta squared (effect size); linear regression (lm); predict(); categorical predictors / dummy coding; SD / variance; proportions  
**Functions:** `aov()`, `coef()`, `data.frame()`, `levels()`, `lm()`, `predict()`, `relevel()`, `summary()`  
**Data:** chickwts

**Question**

The built-in `chickwts` data give chick weights (g) after six weeks on one of six feeds.

(a) Fit `lm(weight ~ feed)`. Which feed is the reference level, and what does the intercept represent? [2]
(b) Interpret the coefficients for horsebean and sunflower. [2]
(c) Show that the model's F-test is the one-way ANOVA. What does R² correspond to? [2]
(d) Make horsebean the reference level and refit. What changes and what doesn't? [2]
(e) Why are the coefficient p-values not a substitute for post hoc tests? [2]

**Model answer (code + interpretation)**

```{r}
levels(chickwts$feed)       # "casein" "horsebean" "linseed" "meatmeal" "soybean" "sunflower"
cm <- lm(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts); summary(cm)
#  (Intercept)   323.58          feedmeatmeal  -46.67 (p = 0.046)
#  feedhorsebean -163.38 (p = 2e-09)   feedsoybean  -77.16 (p = 0.0007)
#  feedlinseed   -104.83 (p = 1.5e-05) feedsunflower  +5.33 (p = 0.81)
#  R² = 0.542, F(5, 65) = 15.36, p = 5.9e-10
summary(aov(weight ~ feed, chickwts))     # F(5, 65) = 15.37, p = 5.94e-10 (identical)
cw <- chickwts; cw$feed <- relevel(cw$feed, ref = "horsebean")
coef(lm(weight ~ feed, data = cw))
#  (Intercept) 160.20  casein 163.38  linseed 58.55  meatmeal 116.71  soybean 86.23  sunflower 168.72
predict(cm, data.frame(feed = levels(chickwts$feed)))    # the six group means
```

**(a)** R uses the first level alphabetically, so **casein** is the reference. The intercept, 323.6 g, is the mean weight of casein-fed chicks. **(b)** Horsebean chicks weigh 163.4 g less than casein chicks on average (160.2 g; p < .001). Sunflower chicks weigh 5.3 g more than casein chicks (328.9 g), a difference that is not significant (p = .81). **(c)** The regression F(5, 65) = 15.36, p < .001, equals the one-way ANOVA F; R² = .54 is the ANOVA's η², the proportion of weight variance explained by feed. **(d)** The intercept becomes the horsebean mean (160.2), and every coefficient is now a difference from horsebean. The fitted group means, residuals, R², F and p are unchanged: it's the same model, described from a different baseline. **(e)** The 5 coefficient tests only compare each feed with the reference (15 pairs are possible), and they are uncorrected for multiple testing. Use `TukeyHSD(aov(weight ~ feed, chickwts))` or Holm-corrected pairwise t-tests.

> Marking: reference + intercept meaning (a); difference-from-reference wording with direction and significance (b); F match + R² = η² (c); what changes vs what is invariant (d); reference-only + no correction (e).


### M6-B5 · A linear mixed model on the course RT dataset [10 marks] {#m6-b5}

**Tests:** Shapiro-Wilk normality test; ANOVA; chi-square test; correlation (Pearson / Spearman); linear regression (lm); linear mixed model (lmer); REML vs ML; singular fit; standard error; IQR / quartiles / outliers; group summaries; contingency table  
**Functions:** `aggregate()`, `anova()`, `factor()`, `lmer()`, `read.csv()`, `residuals()`, `shapiro.test()`, `sort()`, `summary()`, `table()`  
**Data:** BSE658_rt_experiment

**Question**

Load `RT dataset\BSE658_rt_experiment.csv` from your course folder: reaction times (ms) of 30 participants, each tested in a **control** and a **stress** condition, 6 trials per condition.

(a) Describe the data structure. Why is `lm(rt ~ condition)` inappropriate? [2]
(b) Fit a mixed model with condition as a fixed effect and a random intercept for participant. Report and interpret the condition effect. [2]
(c) Test the condition effect with a likelihood-ratio test. [2]
(d) Add a random slope for condition. What happens, and which model do you keep? [2]
(e) Check the residuals. Identify any problem in the data, deal with it, and refit. Do the conclusions change? [2]

**Model answer (code + interpretation)**

```{r}
library(lme4); library(lmerTest)
rt <- read.csv("RT dataset/BSE658_rt_experiment.csv")
rt$condition <- factor(rt$condition); rt$participant <- factor(rt$participant)
table(rt$participant, rt$condition)[1:3, ]        # 6 + 6 trials each, 30 participants → 360 rows
aggregate(rt ~ condition, rt, mean)               # control 509.0, stress 561.3
m1 <- lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = rt); summary(m1)
#  conditionstress 52.31 (SE 9.40, df 329, t = 5.56, p = 5.5e-08); participant SD 42.7, residual SD 89.2
full <- lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 | participant), rt, REML = FALSE)
null <- lmer(rt ~ 1 + (1 | participant), rt, REML = FALSE)
anova(null, full)                                  # chi-sq(1) = 29.67, p = 5.1e-08
m2 <- lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 + condition | participant), data = rt)
#  boundary (singular) fit; random-effect correlation = -1.00
anova(m1, m2, refit = FALSE)                       # chi-sq(2) = 2.42, p = 0.30 → keep m1
shapiro.test(residuals(m1))                        # W = 0.915, p = 2e-13 → non-normal
sort(rt$rt)[1:8]                                   # 135 136 142 160 161 162 178 | 251 ...
r2 <- rt[rt$rt >= 200, ]                          # drop the 7 extreme fast RTs → 353 rows
m3 <- lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = r2); summary(m3)
#  conditionstress 51.08 (SE 7.59, t = 6.73, p = 7.9e-11)
shapiro.test(residuals(m3))                        # p = 0.96 → fixed
```

**(a)** 360 rows, but only 30 independent units: each participant contributes 12 trials, 6 in *each* condition (repeated measures, within-subjects). Rows from the same person share that person's speed, so they are correlated. `lm()` treats 360 rows as independent, which violates independence and mis-states the standard error. **(b)** RT is 52.3 ms slower under stress (SE 9.4, t(329) = 5.56, p < .001), from a control baseline of 509 ms. Participants' baselines vary with SD ≈ 43 ms. **(c)** Comparing ML fits with and without condition: χ²(1) = 29.7, p < .001; adding condition improves the model. **(d)** The random-slope model is **singular** (slope–intercept correlation of −1.00) and doesn't improve fit (χ²(2) = 2.42, p = .30). The data can't support participant-specific stress effects, so keep the random-intercept model. **(e)** Residuals are clearly non-normal (p < .001), caused by 7 implausibly fast responses (135–178 ms; the next fastest is 251 ms). They are outliers, far from the rest of the data. Refit without them, as the regression lecture does with its outlier ("lm() without the outlier"): the residuals become normal (p = .96). The stress effect is essentially unchanged (51.1 ms, p < .001) and more precise (SE 7.6), so the conclusion holds.

> Marking: repeated-measures explanation (a); effect size in ms + test (b); ML refit + χ²(df) (c); singular fit recognised and the simpler model kept (d); outlier diagnosis, refit without the outliers, comparison (e).


## M6 · Quiz 5 Q1 and Quiz 6, fully solved


### M6-PAST1 · Quiz 5 Q1 · PlantGrowth: one-way ANOVA, post hoc test, test all assumptions (normality, homogeneity of variance) and revise as required. {#m6-past1}

**Tests:** t-test; Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Shapiro-Wilk normality test; QQ plot; Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Welch ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; post hoc / multiple comparisons (Holm, Bonferroni); Kruskal-Wallis; eta squared (effect size); chi-square test; normal distribution; confidence interval; SD / variance; mean / median / mode; boxplot; group summaries  
**Functions:** `aggregate()`, `aov()`, `boxplot()`, `by()`, `etaSquared()`, `kruskal.test()`, `leveneTest()`, `mean()`, `oneway.test()`, `pairwise.t.test()`, `qqnorm()`, `residuals()`, `sd()`, `shapiro.test()`, `summary()`, `TukeyHSD()`  
**Data:** PlantGrowth

```{r}
data(PlantGrowth); library(car); library(lsr)
aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
#  ctrl n 10 mean 5.032 sd 0.583 | trt1 4.661 sd 0.794 | trt2 5.526 sd 0.443
boxplot(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth, ylab = "dried weight")
pg <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
summary(pg)                      # F(2, 27) = 4.846, p = 0.0159
etaSquared(pg)                   # eta² = 0.26
TukeyHSD(pg)
#   trt1-ctrl -0.371 [-1.062, 0.320] p = 0.391
#   trt2-ctrl  0.494 [-0.197, 1.185] p = 0.198
#   trt2-trt1  0.865 [ 0.174, 1.556] p = 0.012
pairwise.t.test(PlantGrowth$weight, PlantGrowth$group, p.adjust.method = "holm")   # 0.194, 0.175, 0.013
# assumptions
shapiro.test(residuals(pg))                          # W = 0.966, p = 0.438
by(PlantGrowth$weight, PlantGrowth$group, shapiro.test)   # p = 0.75, 0.45, 0.56
qqnorm(residuals(pg))
leveneTest(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)       # F(2, 27) = 1.12, p = 0.341
# robustness (not required, since both checks pass)
oneway.test(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)      # Welch F(2, 17.13) = 5.18, p = 0.017
kruskal.test(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)     # chi-sq(2) = 7.99, p = 0.018
```

**Answer.** H0: μ_ctrl = μ_trt1 = μ_trt2; H1: not all equal. One-way ANOVA: F(2, 27) = 4.85, p = .016, η² = .26, so mean plant weight differs across conditions. Tukey HSD shows the difference is between the two treatments: trt2 plants were 0.87 g heavier than trt1 plants (95% CI [0.17, 1.56], p = .012). Neither treatment differed significantly from control (trt1 p = .39, trt2 p = .20). **Assumptions:** residuals are normal (Shapiro–Wilk W = 0.97, p = .44; the QQ plot is close to the line), and variances are homogeneous (Levene F(2, 27) = 1.12, p = .34; SD ratio 1.8). Observations are independent plants. No revision is needed. As a check, Welch's ANOVA (p = .017) and Kruskal–Wallis (p = .018) agree. If Levene had failed you would report Welch; if normality had failed, Kruskal–Wallis.

> Where marks go: correct ANOVA with F(df1, df2) and p; a post hoc test with the pair identified; both assumption tests *named, run and interpreted*; and an explicit statement that no revision is needed (or the right fallback).


### M6-PAST2 · Quiz 6 · swiss: Fertility ~ Education + Agriculture + Infant.Mortality. Fit, interpret predictors, check six assumptions, conclude (15 marks). {#m6-past2}

**Tests:** Shapiro-Wilk normality test; QQ plot; Tukey HSD post hoc; chi-square test; linear regression (lm); heteroscedasticity test (ncvTest); VIF / multicollinearity; Cook's distance / influential points; linearity check; linear mixed model (lmer); confidence interval; standard error; SD / variance  
**Functions:** `coef()`, `confint()`, `cooks.distance()`, `lm()`, `ncvTest()`, `par()`, `plot()`, `residualPlots()`, `residuals()`, `shapiro.test()`, `sort()`, `summary()`, `update()`, `vif()`, `which.max()`  
**Data:** swiss

```{r}
library(car)
m <- lm(Fertility ~ Education + Agriculture + Infant.Mortality, data = swiss)
summary(m); confint(m)
```

```text
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)      51.10129   10.99484   4.648 3.18e-05 ***
Education        -0.85697    0.17258  -4.966 1.13e-05 ***
Agriculture      -0.02618    0.07284  -0.359  0.72107
Infant.Mortality  1.49308    0.43880   3.403  0.00145 **
Residual standard error: 8.511 on 43 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.5661,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.5358
F-statistic:  18.7 on 3 and 43 DF,  p-value: 6.517e-08
```

**1. Fit (3).** Fertility = 51.10 − 0.857 Education − 0.026 Agriculture + 1.493 Infant.Mortality. The model is significant: F(3, 43) = 18.7, p < .001. R² = .566, so the three predictors together explain 57% of the variance in fertility across the 47 provinces. Adjusted R² = .536 is slightly lower because it penalises the three predictors; the small gap shows the model is not over-fitted.

**2. Predictors (3).** Education: b = −0.86, p < .001, 95% CI [−1.21, −0.51]. Each extra percentage point of education beyond primary school predicts 0.86 points lower fertility, holding the others constant. Infant mortality: b = 1.49, p = .001, CI [0.61, 2.38]; higher infant mortality goes with higher fertility. Agriculture: b = −0.03, p = .72, CI [−0.17, 0.12], not significant *after accounting for the other predictors*. (On its own Agriculture correlates +.35 with Fertility, but it is strongly correlated with Education, r = −.64, which takes over its effect.) Standardised: Education β = −0.66, Infant.Mortality 0.35, Agriculture −0.05.

```{r}
residualPlots(m)               # Education p = 0.94, Agriculture 0.37, Infant.Mortality 0.45, Tukey 0.89
shapiro.test(residuals(m))     # W = 0.975, p = 0.418
ncvTest(m)                     # chi-sq(1) = 0.93, p = 0.334
# independence: one row per province, no repeated measures → argue from the design
vif(m)                         # 1.75, 1.74, 1.04
cd <- cooks.distance(m); sort(cd, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]   # Sierre 0.196, Glane 0.075, Franches-Mnt 0.063
4 / 47                         # 0.085 → only Sierre exceeds it; none exceeds 1
plot(m, which = 4)             # Cook's distance plot
coef(update(m, subset = -which.max(cd)))   # without Sierre: Edu -0.85, Agri -0.06, IM 1.70 → same conclusions
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(m)
```

| Assumption (6 marks) | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Linearity | residual-vs-fitted shows no curve; curvature tests all p > .37, Tukey p = .89 | met |
| Normality of residuals | QQ close to the line; Shapiro–Wilk W = .975, p = .42 | met |
| Homoscedasticity | no funnel in scale-location; ncvTest χ²(1) = 0.93, p = .33 | met |
| Independence | Each province appears once; there are no repeated measurements of the same unit (the case where the regression lecture says to move to a mixed model). Neighbouring provinces may be similar, which is worth noting as a limitation. | met by design |
| Multicollinearity | all VIF < 2 (Education–Agriculture r = −.64 is the main overlap) | met |
| Influential points | no Cook's D > 1; Sierre (0.20) is above 4/N and V. De Geneve has high leverage (0.45), but refitting without Sierre leaves every conclusion unchanged | acceptable |

**4. Conclusion (3), about 130 words.** "A multiple regression showed that education, agriculture and infant mortality together significantly predicted fertility across 47 Swiss provinces, F(3, 43) = 18.7, p < .001, explaining 57% of the variance (adjusted R² = .54). Education was the strongest predictor: more educated provinces had lower fertility (b = −0.86, p < .001). Higher infant mortality was associated with higher fertility (b = 1.49, p = .001). Agriculture made no unique contribution once the other predictors were controlled (p = .72), probably because it overlaps with education. Linearity, normality, constant variance and multicollinearity were satisfactory, and no single province drove the results. Neighbouring provinces may share regional characteristics, so the observations may not be fully independent. The data are observational and from 1888, so the associations cannot be read as causal."

> The independence check is the one most answers skip. The course checks it from the design: say whether any unit contributes more than one row (here, no: one row per province), and that repeated measures would call for a mixed model.


## M6 · Part A · MCQs with answers (+1 / −0.25)


### M6-A1 · A one-way ANOVA compares 4 groups with 10 participants each. What are the degrees of freedom of F? {#m6-a1}

**Tests:** ANOVA

- A. F(3, 39)
- B. F(4, 36)
- C. F(4, 40)
- **D. F(3, 36)  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** df_b = G − 1 = 3; df_w = N − G = 40 − 4 = 36.


### M6-A2 · In a one-way ANOVA with 3 groups and N = 33, SS_between = 30 and SS_within = 60. What is F? {#m6-a2}

**Tests:** ANOVA; eta squared (effect size); F distribution (pf / qf)  
**Functions:** `pf()`

- A. 2
- **B. 7.5  ← correct**
- C. 0.5
- D. 15

**Answer: B.** MS_b = 30/2 = 15; MS_w = 60/30 = 2; F = 7.5 (p = .002). η² = 30/90 = .33.

```{r}
pf(7.5, 2, 30, lower.tail = FALSE)   # 0.0023
```


### M6-A3 · Load PlantGrowth and run `summary(aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth))`. Which conclusion is correct? {#m6-a3}

**Tests:** ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc  
**Functions:** `aov()`, `summary()`  
**Data:** PlantGrowth

- A. All three groups differ from each other
- B. There is no difference at α = .05
- **C. At least one group mean differs: F(2, 27) = 4.85, p = .016  ← correct**
- D. Both treatments differ from the control

**Answer: C.** ANOVA only says "not all equal". Tukey later shows that only trt2 vs trt1 differs (p = .012).

```{r}
summary(aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth))
```

Output:

```text
            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
group        2  3.766  1.8832   4.846 0.0159 *
Residuals   27 10.492  0.3886
```


### M6-A4 · With 5 groups, why not simply run every pairwise t-test at α = .05? {#m6-a4}

**Tests:** ANOVA

- A. ANOVA has more assumptions
- **B. 10 tests give about a 40% chance of at least one false positive  ← correct**
- C. t-tests need equal n
- D. t-tests cannot compare means

**Answer: B.** 5 groups → 10 pairs; 1 − 0.95¹⁰ = .40. ANOVA plus a corrected post hoc test keeps the familywise rate at .05.


### M6-A5 · Raw p-values from three comparisons are .01, .02 and .04. What are the Holm-adjusted values? {#m6-a5}

**Tests:** post hoc / multiple comparisons (Holm, Bonferroni); contingency table

- A. .03, .06, .12
- B. .01, .02, .04
- C. .03, .04, .12
- **D. .03, .04, .04  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** Sorted: .01 × 3 = .03; .02 × 2 = .04; .04 × 1 = .04. (Bonferroni would give .03, .06, .12.)

```{r}
p <- c(.01, .02, .04)     # already sorted, smallest first
p * c(3, 2, 1)            # Holm: 0.03 0.04 0.04
p * 3                     # Bonferroni: 0.03 0.06 0.12
```


### M6-A6 · A one-way ANOVA gives η² = 0.26. This means: {#m6-a6}

**Tests:** ANOVA; eta squared (effect size); SD / variance; proportions

- A. 26% of participants improved
- B. The groups differ by 0.26 SD
- **C. 26% of the variance in the outcome is explained by group membership  ← correct**
- D. p = .26

**Answer: C.** η² = SS_between / SS_total: a proportion of variance explained (a large effect by the usual benchmarks).


### M6-A7 · Residuals of a one-way ANOVA are normal, but Levene's test gives p = .004. Which analysis should you report? {#m6-a7}

**Tests:** Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Welch ANOVA; Kruskal-Wallis; chi-square test; SD / variance

- **A. oneway.test() (Welch ANOVA)  ← correct**
- B. chisq.test()
- C. kruskal.test()
- D. The ordinary ANOVA, because it is robust

**Answer: A.** Unequal variances alone → Welch's ANOVA. Non-normal residuals → Kruskal–Wallis.


### M6-A8 · In a one-way ANOVA, the normality assumption should be checked on: {#m6-a8}

**Tests:** ANOVA

- A. The group means
- B. The raw outcome pooled across all groups
- **C. The residuals of the model (or each group separately)  ← correct**
- D. The F statistic

**Answer: C.** Pooling raw data from groups with different means can look non-normal even when each group is normal.


### M6-A9 · Load ToothGrowth (dose is numeric: 0.5, 1, 2) and run the code below. How many df does dose get? {#m6-a9}

**Tests:** ANOVA  
**Functions:** `aov()`, `summary()`  
**Data:** ToothGrowth

```{r}
summary(aov(len ~ supp * dose, data = ToothGrowth))
```

- **A. 1, because dose is treated as a numeric covariate  ← correct**
- B. It gives an error
- C. 3
- D. 2, because dose has three levels

**Answer: A.** aov() treats a numeric variable as one continuous predictor. Convert it first: ToothGrowth\$dose <- factor(ToothGrowth\$dose), and dose then has 2 df.


### M6-A10 · In an interaction plot of a two-way ANOVA the lines cross. This suggests: {#m6-a10}

**Tests:** ANOVA; interaction

- **A. An interaction: the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other  ← correct**
- B. Both main effects are significant
- C. The residuals are non-normal
- D. No interaction

**Answer: A.** Parallel lines = no interaction. Crossing lines = a crossover interaction, where the main effects can be zero even though both factors matter.


### M6-A11 · Load warpbreaks and run `summary(aov(breaks ~ wool * tension, warpbreaks))`. Which statement is correct? {#m6-a11}

**Tests:** ANOVA; interaction  
**Data:** warpbreaks

- A. Wool A always breaks less
- B. The interaction is not significant
- C. Only tension matters, because wool p = .058
- **D. The effect of tension on breaks depends on the wool type (interaction p = .021)  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** wool F(1, 48) = 3.77, p = .058; tension F(2, 48) = 8.50, p < .001; wool:tension F(2, 48) = 4.19, p = .021. Wool A at low tension is the outlying cell.


### M6-A12 · `lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)` gives a slope of −5.34. The correct interpretation is: {#m6-a12}

**Tests:** linear regression (lm); SD / variance  
**Data:** mtcars

- A. 5.34% of the variance is explained
- B. Heavier cars cause 5.34% lower mileage
- **C. Each extra 1,000 lb of weight predicts 5.34 mpg less  ← correct**
- D. mpg falls by 5.34 for every 1 lb

**Answer: C.** wt is in 1000 lb. "Predicts", not "causes": the data are observational.


### M6-A13 · In a simple regression the correlation between X and Y is r = −0.868. What is R²? {#m6-a13}

**Tests:** correlation (Pearson / Spearman)

- A. 0.932
- **B. 0.753  ← correct**
- C. −0.868
- D. 0.868

**Answer: B.** In simple regression R² = r² = 0.753 (mtcars mpg ~ wt).


### M6-A14 · In `lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, mtcars)` the wt coefficient is −3.88 (it was −5.34 in mpg ~ wt). Why did it change? {#m6-a14}

**Tests:** linear regression (lm); power / sample size  
**Data:** mtcars

- **A. It is now the effect of weight holding horsepower constant; heavier cars also tend to be more powerful  ← correct**
- B. Adding predictors always halves slopes
- C. A rounding difference
- D. hp is a categorical variable

**Answer: A.** Multiple-regression coefficients are partial effects. Part of weight's simple effect was shared with horsepower.


### M6-A15 · You add a predictor of pure random noise to a regression. What happens to R² and adjusted R²? {#m6-a15}

- A. Neither changes
- B. Both fall
- **C. R² rises slightly (or stays the same); adjusted R² usually falls  ← correct**
- D. Both rise a lot

**Answer: C.** R² can never decrease when a term is added; adjusted R² penalises the extra parameter.


### M6-A16 · `vif(lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + disp, mtcars))` returns wt 4.84, hp 2.74, disp 7.32. What does this indicate? {#m6-a16}

**Tests:** linear regression (lm); VIF / multicollinearity; linearity check  
**Data:** mtcars

- **A. Multicollinearity: disp overlaps strongly with the other predictors (r(wt, disp) = .89)  ← correct**
- B. Influential observations
- C. Heteroscedasticity
- D. Non-normal residuals

**Answer: A.** VIF > 5 is on the high side (slide 16). Consider dropping disp.


### M6-A17 · According to the lecture (slide 11), a point is treated as a potential outlier when Cook's distance is: {#m6-a17}

**Tests:** Cook's distance / influential points; standard error; IQR / quartiles / outliers

- A. Negative
- B. Greater than the residual SE
- **C. Greater than 1 (or, often, greater than 4/N)  ← correct**
- D. Greater than 0.05

**Answer: C.** Then refit without it (subset = -k) and compare the coefficients rather than silently deleting it.


### M6-A18 · `lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)` gives (Intercept) = 5.032, grouptrt1 = −0.371, grouptrt2 = 0.494. What is the mean of trt2? {#m6-a18}

**Tests:** linear regression (lm)  
**Data:** PlantGrowth

- A. 4.661
- **B. 5.526  ← correct**
- C. 0.494
- D. 5.032

**Answer: B.** ctrl is the reference (intercept = its mean); trt2 = 5.032 + 0.494 = 5.526.


### M6-A19 · In `lmer(Reaction ~ days + (1 | Subject), data = d)`, the term `(1 | Subject)` means: {#m6-a19}

**Tests:** linear mixed model (lmer)

- A. Subjects are removed
- B. Each subject gets their own slope for days
- C. Subject is a fixed effect with one level
- **D. Each subject gets their own intercept (baseline), drawn from a normal distribution  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** (1 | g) = random intercept; (1 + x | g) adds a random slope for x.


### M6-A20 · You want to test the fixed effect of attitude with `anova(model_without, model_with)` for two lmer models. How should both models be fitted? {#m6-a20}

**Tests:** ANOVA; linear regression (lm); REML vs ML; standard error

- **A. With REML = FALSE (maximum likelihood)  ← correct**
- B. It doesn't matter
- C. With lm()
- D. With REML = TRUE (the default)

**Answer: A.** REML likelihoods are not comparable when the fixed effects differ; the notebook and slide 9 use REML = FALSE.


## M6 · Which test? quiz (scenario → analysis)


### M6-W1 · Mean yield under 4 fertilisers, 8 plots each. Residuals look normal; Levene p = .30. ANOVA is significant. {#m6-w1}

**Tests:** Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; post hoc / multiple comparisons (Holm, Bonferroni); Kruskal-Wallis

- **A. Report ANOVA + Tukey HSD  ← correct**
- B. Switch to Welch ANOVA
- C. Run 6 t-tests at α = .05
- D. Switch to Kruskal–Wallis

**Answer: A.** Assumptions hold, so the ordinary ANOVA stands; Tukey (or Holm) finds the pairs.


### M6-W2 · One-way ANOVA: Shapiro on residuals p = .40, but Levene p = .003 and the SDs differ 3-fold. {#m6-w2}

**Tests:** Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Shapiro-Wilk normality test; Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Welch ANOVA; post hoc / multiple comparisons (Holm, Bonferroni); Kruskal-Wallis; SD / variance

- **A. Welch ANOVA: oneway.test()  ← correct**
- B. Two-way ANOVA
- C. Ignore it, ANOVA is robust
- D. Kruskal–Wallis

**Answer: A.** Only the equal-variance assumption fails → Welch's ANOVA (+ pairwise.t.test with pool.sd = FALSE).


### M6-W3 · Hospital stays in 5 wards, n = 8 each, heavily right-skewed; residual Shapiro p < .001. {#m6-w3}

**Tests:** Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Shapiro-Wilk normality test; ANOVA; Kruskal-Wallis; correlation (Pearson / Spearman); skewness

- A. One-way ANOVA
- B. Welch ANOVA
- C. Pearson correlation
- **D. Kruskal–Wallis  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** Small, skewed groups with non-normal residuals → Kruskal–Wallis (ANOVA.Rmd: "removing the normality assumption").


### M6-W4 · After a significant 4-group ANOVA you want all 6 pairwise comparisons with simultaneous 95% CIs. {#m6-w4}

**Tests:** t-test; ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; Kruskal-Wallis; linear regression (lm)

- A. Six t.test() calls
- B. kruskal.test()
- **C. TukeyHSD(model)  ← correct**
- D. summary(lm())

**Answer: C.** TukeyHSD gives adjusted p-values and family-wise CIs for every pair.


### M6-W5 · Effect of diet (3 levels) and sex (2) on weight; does the diet effect differ between the sexes? {#m6-w5}

**Tests:** ANOVA; interaction; chi-square test

- A. One-way ANOVA on diet
- B. Two t-tests
- **C. aov(weight ~ diet \* sex): look at diet:sex  ← correct**
- D. χ² test

**Answer: C.** 'Does the effect differ between…' is the interaction term in a two-way ANOVA.


### M6-W6 · Predict house price from floor area, age and distance to the city centre. {#m6-w6}

**Tests:** ANOVA; Kruskal-Wallis; linear regression (lm); linear mixed model (lmer)

- A. Two-way ANOVA
- **B. Multiple regression lm(price ~ area + age + dist)  ← correct**
- C. Mixed model
- D. Kruskal–Wallis

**Answer: B.** Continuous outcome, several numeric predictors → multiple regression.


### M6-W7 · residualPlots() gives a Tukey test p < .001 and the residual-vs-fitted plot is U-shaped. {#m6-w7}

**Tests:** Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Tukey HSD post hoc; linearity check; transformation (log / sqrt); power / sample size

- A. Nothing; R² is high
- B. Use Welch
- C. Remove the largest residual
- **D. Transform (log or Box-Cox) and re-check  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** Curvature = linearity violated. Regression lecture: "If there is severe violation, transform the data. Eg: Log or Box-Cox or powerTransform".


### M6-W8 · vif() returns 9.2 for one predictor and 8.8 for another. {#m6-w8}

**Tests:** Kruskal-Wallis; VIF / multicollinearity; transformation (log / sqrt)

- **A. Drop or combine one of the two correlated predictors  ← correct**
- B. Use Kruskal–Wallis
- C. Log-transform the outcome
- D. Fine, VIF < 10 is always OK

**Answer: A.** VIF > 5 is high (slide 16): the two predictors overlap, so their coefficients are unstable.


### M6-W9 · ncvTest p = .002 and the scale-location plot widens from left to right. {#m6-w9}

**Tests:** chi-square test; heteroscedasticity test (ncvTest); transformation (log / sqrt); power / sample size

- A. Report as is
- **B. Transform Y (log or Box-Cox) and re-check  ← correct**
- C. Add more predictors
- D. Use a χ² test

**Answer: B.** Heteroscedasticity → transform the outcome (regression lecture: "Log or Box-Cox or powerTransform") and re-check.


### M6-W10 · 20 participants each rate 30 faces for attractiveness; does rating depend on face symmetry? {#m6-w10}

**Tests:** ANOVA; linear regression (lm); linear mixed model (lmer)

- A. lm(rating ~ symmetry)
- B. Paired t-test
- **C. lmer(rating ~ symmetry + (1 | participant) + (1 | face))  ← correct**
- D. One-way ANOVA

**Answer: C.** 600 ratings are not independent: crossed random intercepts for raters and faces (like subject and scenario in politeness).


### M6-W11 · lmer with a random slope gives 'boundary (singular) fit', random-effect correlation −1.00. {#m6-w11}

**Tests:** correlation (Pearson / Spearman); linear regression (lm); linear mixed model (lmer); singular fit

- A. Switch to lm()
- **B. Simplify to a random intercept and compare  ← correct**
- C. Report it anyway
- D. Add more random slopes

**Answer: B.** Singular = the random structure is too rich for the data; drop the slope.


### M6-W12 · Does adding two predictors to a regression significantly improve it? {#m6-w12}

**Tests:** Shapiro-Wilk normality test; ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; model selection (step, AIC)

- A. Compare R² by eye
- B. shapiro.test
- C. TukeyHSD
- **D. anova(m_small, m_big)  ← correct**

**Answer: D.** Nested models → F test via anova(); AIC as a second opinion.

## Past papers solved (from the endsem prep guide)


### PP-1 · Quiz 3–4 answer key (17 questions) {#pp-1}

**Tests:** Welch (t-test or ANOVA); chi-square test; McNemar test; correlation (Pearson / Spearman); binomial distribution; power / sample size; standard error; SD / variance

| Q | Ans | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | B | E[X] = np = 20 × 0.3 = 6 |
| 2 | B | χ² becomes more symmetric as df increases |
| 3 | C | P(data at least this extreme \| H0 true) |
| 4 | C | A larger n gives a smaller SE and more power; lowering α to .01 *reduces* power |
| 5 | B | Same 20 people before and after → paired |
| 6 | C | (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 6 |
| 7 | C | `pbinom(3, …)` = P(X ≤ 3) = 0.172 |
| 8 | A | SE ∝ 1/√n; √(100/25) = 2, so half |
| 9 | A | Welch t(55.3) = 1.92, p = .061 > .05 |
| 10 | B | (100 + 0 + 100)/20 = 10 |
| 11 | A | An association, not causation and not means |
| 12 | C | Not significant does not establish that there is no effect |
| 13 | C | Within-person correlation lowers the variance of the differences |
| 14 | A | Row 1 total 40 × column 1 total 35 / 70 = 20 |
| 15 | B | McNemar uses only the discordant cells, 25 and 5 |
| 16 | B | 6 ± 2.064 × 10/√25 = (1.87, 10.13) |
| 17 | A | E = 20 each; χ² = (4 + 64 + 100)/20 = 8.4, df 2, p = .015; critical values 5.99 (5%) and 9.21 (1%) |


### PP-2 · Quiz 5: PlantGrowth ANOVA and sleep paired test {#pp-2}

**Tests:** t-test; one-sample t-test; paired t-test; Welch (t-test or ANOVA); Wilcoxon / Mann-Whitney (non-parametric); Shapiro-Wilk normality test; Levene's test (homogeneity of variance); ANOVA; Welch ANOVA; Tukey HSD post hoc; Kruskal-Wallis; eta squared (effect size); Cohen's d (effect size); chi-square test; confidence interval; power / sample size; SD / variance; mean / median / mode  
**Functions:** `aov()`, `etaSquared()`, `kruskal.test()`, `leveneTest()`, `mean()`, `oneway.test()`, `pwr.t.test()`, `residuals()`, `sd()`, `shapiro.test()`, `summary()`, `t.test()`, `TukeyHSD()`, `with()`  
**Data:** PlantGrowth, sleep

```{r}
a <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
summary(a)                      # F(2, 27) = 4.85, p = .016
etaSquared(a)                   # η² = .26
TukeyHSD(a)                     # only trt2 vs trt1 differs: +0.87, p = .012
shapiro.test(residuals(a))      # p = .44 → normal
leveneTest(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth)  # p = .34 → equal variances
oneway.test(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth) # Welch F(2, 17.1) = 5.18, p = .017 (robustness)
kruskal.test(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth)# χ²(2) = 7.99, p = .018

d <- with(sleep, extra[group == 2] - extra[group == 1])
t.test(d, mu = 0)               # t(9) = 4.06, p = .0028, mean 1.58 h, CI [0.70, 2.46]
mean(d) / sd(d)                 # Cohen's d = 1.28 (large)
pwr.t.test(n = 10, d = 1.28/2, sig.level = .05, type = "paired")  # power = 0.44
shapiro.test(d)                 # p = .033 → check with wilcox.test(d, mu = 0)
```

**Takeaways.** The assumptions held for PlantGrowth, so the right "revision" is to say no change is needed, and to show that Welch and Kruskal–Wallis agree. Treatment 2 beat treatment 1, and neither differed from control. For `sleep`, the effect is large, but with only 10 people a true effect half that size would be detected less than half the time (power 0.44).


### PP-3 · Quiz 6: swiss multiple regression {#pp-3}

**Tests:** Shapiro-Wilk normality test; linear regression (lm); heteroscedasticity test (ncvTest); VIF / multicollinearity; linearity check; SD / variance  
**Functions:** `lm()`, `ncvTest()`, `plot()`, `residualPlots()`, `residuals()`, `shapiro.test()`, `summary()`, `vif()`  
**Data:** swiss

```{r}
m <- lm(Fertility ~ Education + Agriculture + Infant.Mortality, data = swiss)
summary(m)   # F(3, 43) = 18.7, p = 6.5e-08; R² = .566, adj R² = .536
vif(m)                       # 1.75, 1.74, 1.04 → fine
residualPlots(m)             # curvature tests all p > .36 → linear
shapiro.test(residuals(m))   # p = .42 → normal residuals
ncvTest(m)                   # p = .33 → constant variance
# independence: one row per province, no repeated measures → argue from the design
plot(m, which = 4)           # Sierre D = 0.20 > 4/47 = 0.085, but < 1
```

Fertility = 51.10 − 0.857 Education − 0.026 Agriculture + 1.493 Infant.Mortality

**Interpretation.** Education (b = −0.86, p < .001) and infant mortality (b = +1.49, p = .001) are significant after accounting for the other predictors; agriculture is not (p = .72). The model explains about 54% of the variance in fertility (adjusted R²). Linearity, normality, constant variance and collinearity are all fine. Independence holds by design (one row per province, no repeated measures), although neighbouring provinces share regional and cultural factors. Sierre is influential by the 4/N rule; refit without it to check. Limitations: the data are observational, so the coefficients are associations rather than causes; n = 47; aggregated province data invite the ecological fallacy.


### PP-4 · Class assignment: results to check your work against {#pp-4}

**Tests:** Student t-test (equal variances); Welch (t-test or ANOVA); chi-square test; Fisher's exact test; McNemar test; expected counts; confidence interval; proportions

| Problem | Result |
|---|---|
| 1. mpg vs 20 | mean 20.09, t(31) = 0.085, p = .93, CI [17.92, 22.26]; the CI contains 20, agreeing with "not significant" |
| 2. mpg by am | Student t(30) = −4.11, p = .0003; Welch t(18.3) = −3.77, p = .0014. Prefer Welch: the groups have unequal n and SDs |
| 3. sleep paired | t(9) = 4.06, p = .003. Independent t is wrong because the same 10 people took both drugs |
| 4. cyl proportions | observed 11, 7, 14; expected 10.67 each; χ²(2) = 2.31, p = .31 |
| 5. am × cyl | χ²(2) = 8.74, p = .013, but 3 of 6 expected counts are below 5 (smallest 2.84) → Fisher p = .009, same conclusion |
| 6. McNemar | discordant cells 3 and 10; χ²(1) = 2.77, p = .096 → no clear evidence of change |
